content: The document outlines various aspects of hepatitis C (HCV) management, including testing, treatment, and service delivery models, with a focus on decentralization, integration, and task-sharing to improve access and outcomes. Below is a professional interpretation of the content: 1. Interpretation Services: Interpretation in English, French, and Spanish is available for sessions. Users can select their preferred language by clicking the Interpretation button and muting the original audio if needed. 2. Session Recordings and Attendance: Sessions are recorded, and attendance implies consent to recording. Recordings will be shared in English, French, and Spanish. 3. WHO Guidelines for HCV Management: The WHO guidelines emphasize decentralization, integration, and task-sharing to simplify HCV service delivery. Decentralization involves providing HCV testing and treatment at community-based facilities, such as primary care centers, harm reduction sites, prisons, and HIV/ART clinics, ideally at the same location to enhance access. Integration recommends combining HCV services with existing healthcare services, such as primary care, harm reduction programs, and HIV/ART services. Task-sharing involves training non-specialist doctors and nurses to deliver HCV care, expanding access to diagnosis and treatment. 4. Evidence Supporting Decentralization and Integration: A review of 142 studies from 33 countries showed increased uptake of HCV viral load testing, care linkage, and treatment among people who inject drugs (PWID) and prisoners when services were decentralized and integrated. Cure rates (SVR12) were comparable between specialists and non-specialists across all populations and settings. Surveys and interviews highlighted strong support for decentralized and integrated services, with a preference for community-based care close to patients' homes. 5. Implementation Considerations: Service delivery models should be adapted to local contexts and populations. Simplified service delivery principles, such as standardized algorithms, community engagement, and efficient supply management, should be implemented. Decentralization may not be suitable for all settings, particularly in high-income countries with low HCV prevalence, where centralized models may be more efficient. 6. HCV Testing and Diagnostics: Recommendations include focused testing for high-risk populations and general population testing in areas with high HCV prevalence. Point-of-care (POC) HCV RNA testing is recommended as an alternative to laboratory-based assays for diagnosing viremia and confirming cure. Reflex HCV RNA testing following a positive antibody test is encouraged to promote care linkage. 7. Treatment Recommendations for Adolescents and Children: Direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens are highly effective and safe for adolescents and older children, with cure rates (SVR12) exceeding 95%. Early treatment prevents disease progression, liver damage, and stigma while reducing transmission risks. DAAs such as sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (SOF/VEL) and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (G/P) are approved for use in children as young as three years old. 8. Community and Healthcare Worker Preferences: Surveys revealed a strong preference for same-day testing and treatment initiation at the same location, emphasizing convenience and continuity of care. Respondents valued non-judgmental, stigma-free environments for testing and treatment. 9. HCV Service Delivery Innovations: Decentralized models, such as nurse-led DAA initiation pilots, have been implemented in rural areas to address limited access to specialists and diagnostic tools. These models demonstrated high cure rates and consistent patient outcomes, even in resource-limited settings. 10. Challenges and Opportunities: Key challenges include identifying undiagnosed cases (missing millions) and fostering collaboration among stakeholders. Integration of HCV testing with existing platforms for HIV and TB testing offers opportunities for diagnostic synergy. 11. HCV in Malaysia: Malaysia has implemented a decentralized HCV treatment model, achieving significant treatment coverage and cure rates exceeding 90% in the post-DAA era. Efforts include large-scale screening campaigns, compulsory licensing for DAAs, and integration of HCV services into primary healthcare. 12. Conclusion: Decentralized and integrated HCV services are advantageous for improving access and outcomes. A culturally competent approach and same-day testing and treatment are critical to enhancing care linkage. Tailored solutions are needed to address the diverse needs of different populations and settings. This comprehensive approach to HCV management highlights the importance of patient-centered care, innovative service delivery models, and evidence-based guidelines to achieve global elimination goals.
